framework.name: 5 Whys
framework.one_liner: Traces one observed failure down successive layers of cause until the answer is a standard, an incentive or a structure rather than a person, then names the countermeasure that removes it.

slots.label: Problem
slots.description: The observed failure, stated concretely enough to be checked: what happened, to whom, how often. Recurrence evidence belongs here too, because a failure that has been cleared before is the strongest sign that earlier answers stopped too high.

slots.label: Why
slots.description: One causal layer, the answer to 'why did the layer above happen?'. Use level 1..n. The upper layers are usually stated by the speakers; the lower ones, where the answer stops being mechanical and becomes a standard or an incentive, usually have to be inferred.

slots.label: Root cause
slots.description: The systemic cause at the bottom of the chain: a standard, a process, an incentive or a structure whose removal would prevent the whole class of failure, not this instance of it. Almost never stated, because naming it is an admission.

slots.label: Countermeasure
slots.description: What would remove a cause. The fix aimed at a shallow why is usually stated and usually already taken; the countermeasure that reaches the root cause is normally inferred, and it is where the opportunity in the material shows up.

relations.label: because
relations.description: the node it starts from happened because of the node it points to; one step down the causal chain

relations.label: addressed by
relations.description: a cause is removed, or its symptom cleared, by the countermeasure it points to

examples.title: Ohno's machine stoppage: the missing strainer
examples.summary: Taiichi Ohno's own demonstration of the method: a stopped machine, five whys asked in turn, and an answer at the bottom that is a missing part rather than a blown fuse. Extended by two facts Ohno's telling implies, the one-item maintenance sheet and the two earlier fuse replacements, so the sixth why reaches the standard.

source.title: A machine stops on the assembly line
source.attribution: Adapted from Taiichi Ohno, Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production (1978; English edition 1988), the machine-stoppage example that introduces asking why five times.
source.text:
A machine on the assembly line stopped in the middle of the shift. The supervisor did not send for a new fuse; he asked why, and kept asking.
Why did the machine stop? There was an overload and the fuse blew.
Why was there an overload? The bearing was not sufficiently lubricated.
Why was it not lubricated sufficiently? The lubrication pump was not pumping sufficiently.
Why was it not pumping sufficiently? The shaft of the pump was worn and rattling.
Why was the shaft worn out? There was no strainer attached and metal scrap got in.
The team fitted a strainer to the pump inlet and the line restarted. The maintenance sheet for this machine listed a single item, a monthly oil top-up, and the same sheet was in use on the four other machines of this type on the line. The plant's records showed that the fuse on this machine had been replaced twice in the previous year.

nodes.label: Machine stopped mid-shift
nodes.text: A machine on the assembly line stopped in the middle of the shift.
nodes.source_quote: A machine on the assembly line stopped in the middle of the shift

nodes.label: Fuse replaced twice this year
nodes.text: The plant's records showed the fuse on this machine had been replaced twice in the previous year: the same stoppage had already occurred and been cleared twice.
nodes.source_quote: the fuse on this machine had been replaced twice in the previous year

nodes.label: Overload blew the fuse
nodes.text: There was an overload and the fuse blew.
nodes.source_quote: There was an overload and the fuse blew
nodes.source_ref: the team, answer to why 1, sentence 4

nodes.label: Bearing under-lubricated
nodes.text: The bearing was not sufficiently lubricated.
nodes.source_quote: The bearing was not sufficiently lubricated
nodes.source_ref: the team, answer to why 2, sentence 6

nodes.label: Lubrication pump not pumping
nodes.text: The lubrication pump was not pumping sufficiently.
nodes.source_quote: The lubrication pump was not pumping sufficiently
nodes.source_ref: the team, answer to why 3, sentence 8

nodes.label: Pump shaft worn and rattling
nodes.text: The shaft of the pump was worn and rattling.
nodes.source_quote: The shaft of the pump was worn and rattling
nodes.source_ref: the team, answer to why 4, sentence 10

nodes.label: No strainer, metal scrap got in
nodes.text: There was no strainer attached and metal scrap got in.
nodes.source_quote: There was no strainer attached and metal scrap got in
nodes.source_ref: the team, answer to why 5, sentence 12

nodes.label: Sheet lists one item, on 5 machines
nodes.text: The maintenance sheet for this machine listed a single item, a monthly oil top-up, and the same sheet was in use on the four other machines of this type on the line.
nodes.source_quote: The maintenance sheet for this machine listed a single item, a monthly oil top-up, and the same sheet was in use on the four other machines of this type on the line

nodes.label: Routine cannot see filtration
nodes.text: Nothing in the maintenance routine could detect a missing strainer: a sheet whose only item is an oil top-up inspects the oil, not the filtration, so the omission could persist from installation until the shaft failed.
nodes.rationale: The contents of the sheet are stated; that a one-item sheet cannot catch a missing filter, and that the omission was therefore invisible to the routine rather than overlooked by an operator, is the step from the stated condition to its consequence.

nodes.label: The standard omits filtration
nodes.text: The root cause is a standard, not a part: the machine was accepted into service and maintained under a sheet that never mentions filtration, so a missing strainer was not something the routine could ever catch, and the same gap is live on the four sibling machines running the same sheet.
nodes.rationale: Follows from three stated facts held together: no strainer was attached, the sheet's only item is an oil top-up, and that sheet covers four more machines. The missing part explains one stoppage; only the standard explains why the omission survived from installation and why the failure is latent elsewhere.

nodes.label: Replace the fuse (the shallow fix)
nodes.text: Replacing the fuse is the countermeasure you reach by stopping at the first why; the record of two replacements in a year shows it had already been taken twice, clearing the symptom without touching the cause.
nodes.rationale: The scenario states the two replacements but never calls them a countermeasure. Reading the record as two earlier stops at why one is what makes the recurrence meaningful, and it is the inference the framework exists to force.

nodes.label: Fit a strainer to the pump
nodes.text: The team fitted a strainer to the pump inlet and the line restarted.
nodes.source_quote: The team fitted a strainer to the pump inlet and the line restarted

nodes.label: Put filtration in the standard
nodes.text: The countermeasure that matches the root cause changes the standard rather than the pump: a filtration item on the maintenance sheet, a strainer check at installation acceptance, and an audit of the four sibling machines running the same sheet.
nodes.rationale: If the cause is the standard then only the standard can be the remedy, and the shared sheet makes the same failure latent on four other machines, so the countermeasure has to reach them. The scenario states the fix on one pump and nothing beyond it.

edges.source_quote: Why did the machine stop? There was an overload and the fuse blew
Why was there an overload? The bearing was not sufficiently lubricated
Why was it not lubricated sufficiently? The lubrication pump was not pumping sufficiently
Why was it not pumping sufficiently? The shaft of the pump was worn and rattling
Why was the shaft worn out? There was no strainer attached and metal scrap got in

edges.rationale: The scenario states the missing strainer and, separately, what the sheet contains; that the sheet is why the strainer was missing and stayed missing is a sixth why nobody in the scenario asks.
A one-item sheet is stated; that it makes filtration invisible to the routine is read off it.
The blind routine is a consequence of the standard the routine is written from; the standard is the layer below it.
A countermeasure removes its cause: a standard that omits filtration is removed by putting filtration in the standard and auditing the machines that share it.
The scenario reports the strainer being fitted immediately after the missing strainer is found, but never states one as the remedy for the other; the step is close to forced.
Fuse replacement answers the first why and only the first why; the plant record shows it was the countermeasure actually taken twice before.

examples.title: Brian Armstrong on the Coinbase support-bribery breach
examples.summary: The CEO of the breached company walks the causal chain in one answer: customers socially engineered, support agents bribed for their name and address, the agents targeted most being overseas contractors, bribes that would move someone in the United States too, and a 24/7 coverage requirement that keeps the model in place. The layers below that, and the countermeasure that would reach them, are the graph's derived half.

source.episode_title: Crypto Day (Brian Armstrong, Balaji, Chris Dixon, Katie Haun and more)

examples.why_this_episode: Post-mortems in the corpus are usually one layer deep. Here the CEO of the company that was breached is asked how he handled the extortion attack and answers with six distinct causal layers in sequence, none of which blames the bribed agents, plus four countermeasures he actually took. A host then asks the framework's own question aloud, whether this is a technology, talent, oversight or policy issue, which is exactly the fork 5 Whys is built to resolve.

nodes.label: Customers phished out of money
nodes.text: A handful of Coinbase customers were successfully socially engineered into sending their money; Coinbase reimbursed them 100%.
nodes.source_quote: they were able to successfully do that with a handful of customers, which we've reimbursed 100% at this point

nodes.label: $20M extortion demand
nodes.text: Once the attackers realised they had been found out, they demanded $20 million or they would release the stolen customer information.
nodes.source_quote: they sent us this demand for $20 million, or we're going to release all this information

nodes.label: No keys or funds touched
nodes.text: No private keys and no funds were accessed directly by the attacker: the failure was in the support and identity layer, not in custody.
nodes.source_quote: we didn't see any private keys or funds accessed directly by the attacker

nodes.label: Attackers held customer PII
nodes.text: The attackers held personal information on Coinbase customers: name, address, et cetera.
nodes.source_quote: personal information on, on customers, like name, address, et cetera

nodes.label: Support agents were bribed
nodes.text: The attackers bribed some of Coinbase's customer support agents to share that customer information with them.
nodes.source_quote: able to bribe some of our customer support agents

nodes.label: Overseas contractors targeted most
nodes.text: The support agents targeted most were overseas contractors.
nodes.source_quote: The ones that got targeted the most were these overseas contractors and things like that

nodes.label: Bribe outweighs the wage
nodes.text: The money offered as bribes would have been impactful even if the agents had been in the United States.
nodes.source_quote: some of the money being offered as bribes would have been pretty impactful even in the United States if people were there

nodes.label: 24/7 coverage forces the model
nodes.text: Coinbase needs 24/7 support coverage, so moving all of it into the United States and paying people more is not a perfect solution and does not fully solve the problem.
nodes.source_quote: We need to have 24-7 coverage, et cetera. So it's not perfect solution to like just move it all in the US and pay people more.

nodes.label: Agents must read PII to work
nodes.text: Resolving a support ticket requires reading the customer's identity, so every agent, in-house or contracted, holds standing read access to that data; a bribe buys an ordinary lookup rather than an intrusion.
nodes.rationale: Armstrong describes agents sharing name and address, not any system being broken into, and says the controls limited the scope of what was reached rather than preventing the reads. Standing task-level access is the only arrangement in which bribery alone yields customer identity data, and it is nowhere stated.

nodes.label: Vendors held the same access
nodes.text: The exposure was not only in Coinbase's own systems: third-party vendors it works with had to be pushed to hit a higher security bar.
nodes.source_quote: There's vendors that we work with that we needed to push them to hit a higher bar as well

nodes.label: Controls limited scope, not access
nodes.text: Coinbase already had controls that limited the scope of what the bribed agents could reach, but, in Armstrong's words, it obviously did not do enough.
nodes.source_quote: luckily we had, we had some good controls already, which limited the scope of it, but we obviously didn't do enough

nodes.label: Data worth more than its custodian
nodes.text: The root cause is a standing mismatch rather than a bribed individual: a 24/7, partly outsourced support function must hold customer identity data whose value to an attacker is orders of magnitude above the wage of the person holding it, and access is granted to people rather than to tasks. Relocating the people changes the price of a bribe; it does not remove the exposure.
nodes.rationale: Holds together four stated facts that no speaker joins: the 24/7 constraint that keeps support distributed, the bribe-versus-wage economics, the vendor gap, and the admission that scope-limiting controls were not enough. None of them alone is the cause; the arrangement that makes all four true at once is the layer below the last stated why.

nodes.label: Host: CX entirely code
nodes.text: A host proposes that a more secure customer-experience function would in future be entirely code, or at least carry AI oversight of every interaction.
nodes.source_quote: is there's a world in the future where a more secure CX function would be entirely code

nodes.label: Relocate support operations
nodes.text: Coinbase relocated some of its customer support operations.
nodes.source_quote: We did relocate some of our customer support operations

nodes.label: $20M bounty as deterrent
nodes.text: Coinbase flipped the extortion demand and put out a $20 million bounty for information leading to the attackers' arrest and conviction.
nodes.source_quote: we put out a 20 million dollar bounty for any information leading to their arrest

nodes.label: 60% of inquiries answered by AI
nodes.text: About 60% of Coinbase's customer support inquiries are now answered by AI.
nodes.source_quote: Our customer support, I think maybe 60% of inquiries are being answered by AI now

nodes.label: Take PII out of the human path
nodes.text: The countermeasure that matches the root cause removes identity data from the human path: tickets resolved against tokenised references with per-ticket, time-boxed grants, so an agent, contractor or vendor can act on an account without ever reading name and address, and the bribe buys nothing worth paying for.
nodes.rationale: Follows from the root cause: if the exposure is standing human access to plaintext identity data, only removing that access removes it. The transcript states the scope-limiting controls and the vendor gap but never names access redesign, which is what the countermeasure slot forces you to write down.
nodes.idea: Insider-threat tooling for outsourced support: a PII-redacting agent console with per-ticket, time-boxed access grants, sold to fintechs whose BPO vendors are in practice their security perimeter.

nodes.label: AI support as a security control
nodes.text: The 60% AI resolution rate is already a security control and not only a margin story: an agent that cannot be bribed removes part of the human surface, and the human-in-the-loop cases that remain carry the whole residual risk.
nodes.rationale: Armstrong answers a security question with the automation number and the remark that the AI is not going to get bribed, which makes automation rate a control metric. That reframing, and the corollary that the remaining human cases concentrate the risk, is not stated.
nodes.idea: Sell AI customer support to regulated fintechs as an insider-threat control with an audited automation rate rather than as a cost saving: the buyer is the security owner, not the support budget.

nodes.label: Continuous vendor attestation
nodes.text: Because a vendor's controls are in practice the company's controls, the countermeasure extends past a contractual bar to continuous evidence: standing proof of which vendor staff can read which customer fields, rather than a point-in-time attestation.
nodes.rationale: Armstrong states that vendors had to be pushed to a higher bar but not how a bar is kept once pushed. The step from a one-off push to continuous verification is an inference, and a contestable one, since a contractual bar plus an annual audit is the industry's current answer.
nodes.idea: Continuous vendor-access attestation for support BPOs: live evidence of which vendor staff can read which customer fields, priced as a control that the regulator and the enterprise customer can both see.

edges.source_quote: Attackers want this information because they want to text people, call people, try to socially engineer them and to get them to send their money
able to bribe some of our customer support agents and to share with them like personal information on, on customers
The ones that got targeted the most were these overseas contractors and things like that

edges.rationale: Armstrong gives the size of the bribes immediately after saying which agents were targeted most, but never states the first as the reason for the second; that the wage gap is what made those agents the ones approached is the standard reading of the two lines together.

The 24/7 requirement is given as the reason support cannot simply move to the United States, which implies it is also why the work sits with overseas contractors in the first place. The constraint is stated; this causal step is not.
The bribe produced name and address with no system broken into, which only works if the agents can read that data as a matter of routine.
Controls that limit the scope of a breach without removing the access are exactly what standing read access looks like from the inside; joining the admission to the mechanism is the inference.

Armstrong says the exposure was not only in Coinbase's own systems. That vendor staff hold the same standing access, and that this is why the vendors had to be pushed, is the reading, not the statement.
The staffing model that 24/7 coverage forces is one of the four conditions the root cause names.
Scope-limiting controls that were not enough is the access half of the root cause, stated by the person who owns it.
The vendor perimeter extends the same mismatch to people Coinbase does not employ.
The bribe-versus-wage economics is the value half of the mismatch: the data is worth far more to the attacker than the custodian is paid.

edges.source_quote: We did relocate some of our customer support operations. The ones that got targeted the most were these overseas contractors
We decided to flip it and as you probably saw, we put out a $20 million bounty for any
the 60% of inquiries being answered by AI now, I mean, they're not going to get bribed

edges.rationale: The host offers an all-code CX function in answer to the security question; that it is a countermeasure to bribery specifically, because a code path has nobody to bribe, is the reading of it.
Removing standing human access to identity data is the only countermeasure that acts on the mismatch itself rather than on its price.
Every inquiry resolved without a human removes a custodian from the population that can be bribed.
The mismatch reaches vendor staff, so a countermeasure that stops at Coinbase's own systems leaves it in place.
